paragraphs: It is stated in a wondrous midrash that tefillin are worn only on Shabbat — which is strange, for one certainly wears tefillin on the other days of the week as well! Rabbi Shalom Mordechai Schwadron (the Maharsham), of blessed memory, explained this in his "Likkutei Shoshanim" at the end of his book "Karnayim" — see there. But I heard in the name of the Gaon Rabbi Akiva Eiger, of blessed memory, that he explained "Shabbat" (שב"ת) as an acronym for "place of hair, place of the swelling" (שער, תפוח): the tefillin shel rosh (head-tefillin) must be placed on the place where hair grows, and the tefillin shel yad (hand-tefillin) must be placed on the lower joint near the shoulder, on the raised flesh — the swelling called the "kiboret," a term related to "kiburei dahinei," meaning a gathering of dates, and likewise meaning a gathering of flesh, i.e. the flesh that swells. One must therefore caution the people about this, for regarding the head-tefillin especially there are many who err and are not careful about it. One must be careful that the lower edge of the titura (the base of the box) rests exactly at the start of the roots of the hair, since the titura too is part of the tefillin. A person with long hair lying down to the middle of the forehead — even though he places the tefillin on top of the hair — does not fulfill the mitzvah this way, for what is required is placement from the actual start of the hair roots and upward; the measure of this place extends to where an infant's skull is still soft. If he placed it lower, at the point where the hair roots end, this follows the way of the Karaites and he has not fulfilled the mitzvah, and is even punished for it. However, an elderly man whose hair has fallen out, and likewise a bald man — even though they now have no hair on their head — should place the tefillin at the place where hair used to grow, which is discernible to the eye, since there is a visible difference between the skin of baldness and skin where hair never naturally grows at all. Know also that in my holy work "Makabtziel" I cited the words of the author of "Chayei Adam," who wrote that if most of the box rests on the place of hair and only a small part rests on the forehead, at the point where the hair roots end, one has not fulfilled his obligation, for what is required is that the entire box rest on the place of hair. And I cited there the words of Rav "Nachal Eshkol" in the book "HaEshkol," at the end of the laws of tefillin, who brought the words of the aforementioned "Chayei Adam" and concurred with this ruling. I also recalled there what I had written, with Heaven's help, in my holy work "Rav Berakhot," page 187, regarding the law of the parashiyot [Torah passages] that protrude outside the box. I debated these matters at length, and in the end I concluded, in accordance with the view of "Chayei Adam," of blessed memory, that the entire box, in its entirety, must rest on the place of hair.

clarification.explanation: The midrash states, puzzlingly, that tefillin are worn only on "Shabbat" — seemingly a wonder, since one certainly wears tefillin on the other days of the week too! Some explain that "Shabbat" here is an acronym: "se'ar" (hair) and "tapuach" (swelling) — the head-tefillin must be placed on the place of the hair, and the hand-tefillin must be placed on the raised, swelling flesh (called the "kiboret") on the lower part of the arm near the shoulder. One must caution the public, especially regarding the head-tefillin, since many are not careful enough: the lower edge of the "titura" (the base of the box) must rest exactly at the start of the hair roots. Someone with long hair reaching down to the middle of the forehead is still obligated to place the tefillin at the true start of the hair roots (not wherever appears to be covered by hair due to its length), because the place is measured up to the point where an infant's skull is still soft. If he placed it lower than that, this is the way of the Karaites and he has not fulfilled the mitzvah, and is even punished for it. An elderly man whose hair has fallen out, or a bald man, still places the tefillin at the place where the hair originally was, which can be distinguished by sight from skin that naturally never grows hair at all. Rabbi Yosef Chaim also rules that the entire box of the tefillin (not merely most of it) must rest exactly at the place of the hair, and it is not sufficient for most of it to be on the place of hair with only a small part on the forehead.
takeaways: The head-tefillin must rest exactly at the start of the hair roots (up to the point of the infant's soft skull), not lower, even if the hair is long.
The entire box of the tefillin (not merely most of it) must rest on the place of the hair — this is a strict ruling many are not careful about.

paragraphs: The knot of the head-tefillin, too, must rest on a place of hair, at the height of the nape of the neck, which is the end of the skull bone, opposite the face. If one places the knot on the neck itself, he has accomplished nothing, since that is not called the "nape."

clarification.explanation: The knot of the strap of the head-tefillin must also rest at a place that has hair — at the height of the nape of the neck, which is the end of the skull bone (the point opposite the face). If one places the knot on the neck (below the true nape), he has not fulfilled the mitzvah at all.
takeaways: The knot of the head-tefillin must be at the height of the nape (on a place of hair), not on the neck.

paragraphs: One must position the head-tefillin so that the box sits at the exact center of the width of the head, so that it is between the eyes; likewise, the knot must be exactly at the center of the nape, not tilted to either side. Also, the place on the knot that appears in the shape of the letter dalet must face outward, not toward the nape. The same law applies to the knot of the hand-tefillin: one must be careful that it does not turn over. If it did turn over, it is proper to fast; and if the fast is too difficult for him, he may redeem it with charity.

clarification.explanation: One must position the head-tefillin so that the box (the kitzitza) sits exactly at the center of the width of the head, between the eyes. Likewise, the knot must be exactly at the center of the nape, not tilted to one side. The shape resembling the letter dalet formed by the strap around the knot must face outward, not toward the nape. The same law applies to the knot of the hand-tefillin — one must be careful that it does not turn over; and if it did turn over, it is proper to fast (and if the fast is too difficult, one may redeem it with charity).
takeaways: Exact placement: the box of the head-tefillin between the eyes, the knot at the center of the nape with the "dalet" shape facing outward.
If the knot of the hand-tefillin turns over, it is proper to fast a day, or to redeem the fast with charity.

paragraphs: The boxes and the straps of both the head-tefillin and the hand-tefillin must be black — this is a halacha given to Moshe at Sinai. Therefore, if they turned pale from age, one must blacken them again; but if a non-Jew blackened them, they are invalid. The black side of the straps must face outward. If the strap that goes around the head, or likewise the strap with which the box is tied, became turned over, one should fast for one day. As for Rav Huna, who fasted forty days on account of this, that was an act of exceptional piety on his part, not an obligation. It is also good to be careful regarding the straps of the head-tefillin that hang down to the chest and navel, and likewise the strap of the hand-tefillin that is wound around the arm, that they not become turned over. And although according to the Kabbalah the straps are blackened on both sides — front and back — black as a raven, as mentioned in "Sha'ar HaKavanot" by our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, we have not followed this practice. I inquired about the custom of the pious in the Holy City [Jerusalem], may it be rebuilt and established speedily in our days, and was told that some are careful to blacken both front and back, while others do not concern themselves with this.

clarification.explanation: The boxes and straps of both the head-tefillin and hand-tefillin must be black — this is a halacha given to Moshe at Sinai. If they faded from use, one must blacken them again; but if a non-Jew blackened them, they are invalid. The black side of the straps must face outward. If any strap (the one around the head, or the one with which the box is tied) turned over, one should fast for one day (the fact that Rav Huna fasted forty days over this was his own exceptional measure of piety, not an obligation for everyone). One must also be careful with the long straps hanging down to the chest and navel, and with the strap wound around the arm, that they not turn over. Although according to the Kabbalah there is a method of blackening the straps on both sides (front and back) as taught by the Ari, of blessed memory, that was not the practice where Rabbi Yosef Chaim lived; some of the pious in Jerusalem are indeed careful about this.
takeaways: The boxes and straps of the tefillin must be black, and must be blackened by a Jew (not a non-Jew).
A strap turning over (the non-black side facing outward) requires a day's fast (or redemption with charity).

paragraphs: Nothing may intervene between the tefillin and one's flesh, whether regarding the boxes or the straps. If there is dirt, one must wash it off. One who wears eyeglasses must be careful not to tuck them between the strap and his flesh, but rather to tuck them between the strap and his hat; and if this is not possible otherwise, he must be careful about this at least during the reading of the Shema and its blessings and the Amidah prayer. The later authorities, of blessed memory, raised doubts concerning those who grow their hair very long on their heads, since — being so overgrown — one cannot say this is their normal growth, according to the view of the Rosh, of blessed memory; and also according to the view of the Rashba, of blessed memory, such abundant hair is like a wound-dressing and constitutes an interposition when the tefillin are worn over it. They likewise raised doubts about head hair that hangs down below its natural place of growth, that it too is not its natural growth-place and constitutes an interposition. One must caution the masses about such matters as much as possible, given the greatness and preciousness of this mitzvah.

clarification.explanation: Nothing may intervene between the tefillin (whether the boxes or the straps) and the flesh. If there is dirt, it must be washed off. One who wears eyeglasses must be careful not to tuck them between the strap and his flesh, but rather between the strap and his hat; and if this cannot be avoided otherwise, he must at least be careful about it during the reading of the Shema and its blessings and the Amidah prayer. The later authorities discussed the case of someone with very abundant hair on his head — if it is excessively thick, there is concern that it constitutes an interposition between the tefillin and the head (unless this is the ordinary condition for people generally). They likewise discussed hair that hangs down below its place of natural growth, which may also constitute an interposition. One must caution the public about these matters as much as possible, given the great importance of this mitzvah.
takeaways: Nothing (eyeglasses, dirt) may be placed between the tefillin and the flesh, at least during the reading of the Shema and the Amidah prayer.
Overly thick or overly long hair at the place of the tefillin may be considered an interposition and invalidate the mitzvah.

paragraphs: We have already said above that the hand-tefillin are placed on the arm, on the lower joint near the shoulder, on the raised flesh called the kiboret, and one must not place it lower than the kiboret, since what is required is placement opposite the heart, and the kiboret is aligned opposite the heart. Therefore one must tilt the hand-tefillin slightly toward the body, so that when the arm is bent downward, the hand-tefillin will be exactly aligned opposite the heart. Even within the aforementioned lower joint itself, one must be careful not to place it in the upper half of that joint, near the armpit, even though raised flesh extends there too; rather, one should place it in the half near the middle joint, at the place of raised flesh found there. According to the Gaon Rabbeinu Eliyahu of Vilna (the Gra), of blessed memory, any place of raised flesh is valid, including that part extending into the half near the armpit — see "Chayei Adam," Klal 14, letter yud, and other later authorities. And in my holy work "Makabtziel" I concluded, with Heaven's help, that ideally one should be concerned for the view of the authorities who hold that in the second half one may not place tefillin even on the raised flesh reaching there. Therefore, one who wears both Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam tefillin together must be careful to make them small, so that he can place them on the swollen flesh in the first half of the joint; and where this is not possible, one may rely on the view of the aforementioned Gaon Rabbi Eliyahu of Vilna, who holds that the entire flesh of the kiboret is fit for placing tefillin upon it.

clarification.explanation: As mentioned, the hand-tefillin are placed on the lower joint of the arm near the shoulder, on the raised flesh (the "kiboret") — not lower than that, because they must be aligned opposite the heart, and the kiboret is aligned opposite the heart. Therefore one must tilt the tefillin slightly toward the body, so that when the arm is bent downward, the tefillin will be exactly opposite the heart. Even within the lower joint itself, one must not place it in the upper half (near the armpit), but rather in the half near the middle joint, at the raised flesh found there. One opinion (the Gra) is more lenient and validates the entire area of raised flesh, including the part near the armpit. Rabbi Yosef Chaim rules that ideally one should be concerned for the stricter view — therefore one who wears both Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam tefillin together should be careful to make them small so they fit in the correct place, and only when there is no other option may one rely on the Gra.
takeaways: Hand-tefillin should be placed on the lower-middle part of the arm (the kiboret), not on the upper part near the armpit, and should be tilted slightly so as to be opposite the heart; therefore one who wears Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam together should make them small so they can be placed there, relying on the Gra's leniency only when there is no other option.

paragraphs: The hand-tefillin are placed on the left hand, which is the weaker, feebler hand. A left-handed person (whose right hand is weak) — if he does all his work with his left hand — should place the hand-tefillin on his left hand, which is functionally the "right" for every person. If he uses both hands equally, he should place it on the ordinary left hand. If he writes with his right hand but does all his other actions with his left hand, or writes with his left hand but does his other actions with his right — there is a dispute: some say the determining factor is the weaker hand, since what is required is a "feeble hand"; and some say that the hand with which one writes is considered the "right hand" for this purpose, and one places the tefillin on the hand opposite it, since Scripture juxtaposes "and you shall bind them" with "and you shall write them" — just as writing is with the right hand, so too binding is with the right hand; and since binding is done with the right hand, it follows that placement is on the left — meaning, on the hand with which one writes, one must tie the tefillin on the hand opposite it. All this is written and explained in the words of Maran [Rabbi Yosef Karo], of blessed memory, Siman 27, Se'if 6 — see there. However, Rav "Shalmei Tzibbur," page 40, column 3, wrote that the Kabbalist Rav Maharai Tzemach, of blessed memory, in his book "Zer Zahav," elaborated at length with proofs that a left-handed person may not deviate from everyone else, so as not to alter the higher order — see there; and he cited his words in "Pitchei Teshuvah" and also in the book "Me'ir La'aretz." And indeed, the words of Rav Maharai Tzemach, of blessed memory, are correct according to reasons based on the Kabbalah, and a great man has said a reasonable thing. Therefore I concluded, with Heaven's help, in my holy work "Makabtziel," that a left-handed person should always follow the view of Maran, of blessed memory, and all the authorities who rule simply, who hold that if he does all his work with his left hand, he should place the hand-tefillin on his left hand (which is the "right" hand for every person), and pray wearing this pair of tefillin. But after the prayer, he should put on tefillin on the ordinary left hand as well, without reciting the blessing with God's Name and Kingship, but rather contemplating the Name and Kingship in his heart, and reciting the Shema without blessings, intending to fulfill his obligation according to the view of the Maharitz, of blessed memory. However, this requires making two sets of hand-tefillin — one fitted for placement on the right hand and one fitted for placement on the left hand — since it is impossible to use one set for both hands, because of the knot of the letter yud, which would come out on the outside if the tefillin were turned over. And although I inquired about the custom of the Holy City, may it be rebuilt and established speedily, and was told that their custom is not to be concerned for the view of the Maharitz mentioned above, nevertheless I say that a God-fearing person should fulfill this mitzvah according to all views, since it is a precious mitzvah, and all the more so since this reasoning is sensible according to the Kabbalah. And there I cited the words of Rav Chikrei Lev, of blessed knowledge, in the manner he wrote in Siman 27, letter heh, and I raised objections to his words, and the matter is simple. However, if the person in question writes with the ordinary right hand [i.e., is not left-handed], one may simply instruct him to rely on the view of the one who says that the hand with which one writes is considered the "right" hand, even though he does all his other actions with the hand opposite it, and he should place the tefillin on the left hand, which is the ordinary left hand for everyone. In this case there is no need to trouble him to place tefillin a second time according to the dissenting view, because in such a case, where he writes with the ordinary right hand, even the authorities who rule simply hold that this suffices, following the writing hand — since the hand with which one writes is considered the right hand, even though he does all his other actions with the hand opposite it. And if he wishes, even in this case, to place tefillin a second time in order to fulfill his obligation according to all views, blessing will come upon him.

clarification.explanation: The hand-tefillin are placed on the left hand (the weaker, "feeble" hand). A left-handed person (whose left hand functions as the dominant hand, the way the right hand functions for most people) who does all his work with his left hand places the hand-tefillin on his left hand (which is functionally the "right" hand for every person). One who is equally skilled with both hands places it on the ordinary left hand. In a more complex case — someone who writes with the right hand but does his other work with the left (or vice versa) — there is a dispute: some say the weaker hand determines it, and some say the writing hand is considered "right," so the tefillin are placed on the hand opposite it. Rabbi Yosef Chaim discusses the view of the Kabbalist Maharai Tzemach, that a left-handed person must never deviate from everyone else's order, his reasoning being grounded in the Kabbalah, and arrives at a practical conclusion: a left-handed person should follow Maran and the straightforward halachic authorities (placing the tefillin on his left hand, which is the "right" for everyone, and praying that way), but after the prayer he should also put on tefillin on the ordinary left hand (without a blessing invoking God's Name and Kingship, only contemplating it in his heart, and reciting the Shema without blessings) — so as to fulfill the mitzvah according to all views; for this he needs two sets of hand-tefillin (one suited to each hand; only one set of head-tefillin is needed), since one set cannot be used for both hands — the knot of the letter yud would come out on the outside if it were turned over. Regarding someone who writes with the ordinary right hand (not left-handed), one may simply rely on the view that the writing hand is considered the right hand, without troubling him to place tefillin twice.
takeaways: A left-handed person (who does his work with his left hand) places the hand-tefillin on his left hand (which is the "right" for everyone); to fulfill the mitzvah according to all views, it is proper (though not obligatory) to also place a second set of tefillin on the other hand without a blessing.
One who writes with the ordinary right hand but does other things with the left may rely on the view that the writing hand determines the placement, without a double placement.

paragraphs: The time for putting on tefillin in the morning begins from when one can recognize an acquaintance at a distance of four amot. It is good to delay somewhat rather than to do it early. If one erred and put on tefillin while it was still night and recited the blessing over them, he need not repeat the blessing when daylight comes, as noted in "Eliyah Rabbah," small paragraph 3, and other later authorities, of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: The time for putting on tefillin in the morning begins from when one can recognize an acquaintance at a distance of four amot. It is good to be careful to delay this time slightly rather than to do it early. One who erred and put on tefillin before dawn, and recited the blessing over them, need not repeat the blessing when daylight comes.
takeaways: The time for tefillin begins when one can recognize an acquaintance at a distance of four amot; it is good to delay slightly rather than do it early.

paragraphs: One should not remove the hand-tefillin entirely until he has removed the head-tefillin, for we hold that as long as possible there should be two [tefillin] between your eyes. This is the order of their removal: first he removes the windings on the finger, and he also removes two or three windings from his arm, so that the removal parallels the placement — since he put on the hand-tefillin first — hinting at the verse, "as they encamped, so they journeyed" (Numbers 2:17). But he does not remove the hand-tefillin entirely, because he must fulfill what is said, "and for frontlets between your eyes" (Exodus 13:16), meaning that as long as possible there should be two between your eyes. Therefore, after he has removed two or three windings of the hand-tefillin from the arm, he then removes the head-tefillin while standing, and afterward he sits and removes the hand-tefillin entirely while seated, just as he put it on while seated. And although the removal of the windings before the removal of the head-tefillin is not explicitly stated in the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, nevertheless our teacher Rav Shmuel Vital, of blessed memory, established this practice in order to reconcile the words of the Ari, of blessed memory, with the words of the Gemara, and wrote that it seemed to him that he had seen his father, our teacher Rav Chaim Vital, of blessed memory, practice this way, as he wrote in his gloss on "Sha'ar HaKavanot" and also in his book "Chemdat Yisrael" — see there. And I say that there is a compelling proof for this from the words of our teacher [the Ari], of blessed memory, himself, in "Sha'ar HaKavanot," at the end of the text of the prayer, page 51, column 4, where he wrote that my teacher, of blessed memory, would remove the head-tefillin from his head, etc., and afterward remove the hand-tefillin, etc. — see there. However, reason dictates, according to the mystical secret of these matters, that the removal must parallel the placement: one must remove the windings on the finger while standing, then sit and remove the three windings of the arm while seated (just as he wound them while seated), and afterward stand and remove the head-tefillin while standing. And from the book "Chesed LaAlafim," Siman 28, letter gimel, it appears that one removes the three windings of the arm while standing as well — see there. And our teacher the Chida, of blessed memory, in "Tziporen Shamir," wrote, "He removes the windings of the finger while standing," and did not mention the windings of the arm at all — see there. It appears that one should be precise to remove the three windings of the arm while seated, just as he put them on while seated, as we have written.

clarification.explanation:
When removing the tefillin, one should not remove the hand-tefillin entirely until first removing the head-tefillin, for we hold that "as long as possible there should be two between your eyes." This is the order of removal: first one removes the windings on the finger, and also two or three windings from the arm — so that the removal parallels the placement (since one puts on the hand-tefillin first), hinting at the verse "as they encamped, so they journeyed." But one does not remove the hand-tefillin entirely, in order to fulfill "and for frontlets between your eyes" — meaning that as long as possible there should be two between one's eyes; therefore after removing two or three windings from the arm, one removes the head-tefillin while standing, and then sits and removes the hand-tefillin entirely while seated, just as he put it on while seated.
Although removing the windings before the head-tefillin is not explicit in the words of the Ari, of blessed memory, our teacher Rav Shmuel Vital, of blessed memory, established this practice in order to reconcile the Ari's words with the Gemara, and wrote that it seemed to him he had seen his father, Rav Chaim Vital, of blessed memory, practice this way (in his gloss on "Sha'ar HaKavanot" and in his book "Chemdat Yisrael"); and the Ben Ish Chai adds that there is compelling proof for this from the Ari's own words in "Sha'ar HaKavanot" (at the end of the text of the prayer), where it is written that the Ari himself would remove the head-tefillin first and afterward the hand-tefillin.
However, reason dictates, according to the mystical secret of these matters, that the removal should parallel the placement: remove the windings of the finger while standing; sit and remove the three windings of the arm while seated (as he wound them while seated); then stand and remove the head-tefillin while standing. From "Chesed LaAlafim" (Siman 28) it appears that one removes the windings of the arm while standing as well, and the Chida, of blessed memory (in "Tziporen Shamir"), wrote to remove the windings of the finger while standing and did not mention the windings of the arm at all; in practice, it appears one should be precise to remove the three windings of the arm while seated, as he put them on.
takeaways: One does not remove the hand-tefillin entirely until removing the head-tefillin ("as long as possible there should be two between your eyes").

The order of removal parallels the placement: the finger windings while standing; sit and remove two or three windings of the arm while seated as one wound them; stand and remove the head-tefillin while standing; then sit and remove the hand-tefillin entirely while seated.

"Chesed LaAlafim" implies the arm windings are also removed while standing, and the Chida did not mention them at all; in practice, it appears one should be precise to remove them while seated, as one put them on.

paragraphs: It is proper to remove the head-tefillin and the tallit with the left hand, which is the weaker hand, to demonstrate that separating from them is difficult, as the later authorities, of blessed memory, have written. One should not remove the tefillin until after [reciting] "Aleinu LeShabeach" and "Al Ken Nekaveh Lach." It is the custom of the sages to kiss the tefillin at the time of putting them on, at the time of removing them, and when placing them into their bag, out of love for the mitzvah.

clarification.explanation: It is proper to remove the head-tefillin and the tallit with the left hand (the weaker hand), to demonstrate that it is difficult to part from them. One should not remove the tefillin before finishing the prayers "Aleinu LeShabeach" and "Al Ken Nekaveh Lach." It is the custom of the sages to kiss the tefillin when putting them on, when removing them, and when placing them into their bag, out of love for the mitzvah.
takeaways: One should remove the tefillin with the left hand, only after finishing "Aleinu LeShabeach," and it is the custom of the sages to kiss the tefillin when putting them on, removing them, and placing them into the bag.

paragraphs: One should not remove the tefillin until he has first studied [Torah] while wearing them — whether much or little — for a person will not merit to acquire the three parts of the soul (nefesh, ru'ach, neshamah) unless he studies Torah while wearing tefillin, and all the more so if he studies while wearing the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam, as "Machazik Berachah" wrote in the name of the Maharam Peretz, of blessed memory — see there.

clarification.explanation: One should not remove the tefillin before studying at least a little Torah while wearing them — whether much or little — for a person does not merit to acquire the three parts of the soul (nefesh, ru'ach, neshamah) unless he studies Torah while wearing tefillin, and all the more so if he also studies while wearing the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam.
takeaways: One should study a little Torah while still wearing tefillin, before removing them, in order to merit the fullness of soul connected to this mitzvah.

paragraphs: However, on the first day [of mourning] it is forbidden to put on tefillin, but on the second day one is obligated to do so immediately after sunrise. If one's relative died on one day and was buried on another, it is forbidden to put on tefillin on the day of burial; and likewise it is forbidden to put on tefillin on the day the news of a close relative's death reaches him. However, if his relative died during a festival — so that the counting of the seven days of mourning begins only after the festival — he is obligated to put on tefillin already on the first day [of mourning]. The custom has spread in the Holy City of Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt and established, and also here in the city of Baghdad, for the mourner to put on the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam, following the ruling of our teacher the Rashash, and not according to our teacher the Chida, of blessed memory, who wrote that "sitting and not acting is preferable."

clarification.explanation: On the first day (the day of burial, which is the first day of mourning), a mourner may not put on tefillin, but on the second day he is obligated to put them on immediately after sunrise. If a relative died on one day and was buried on another, it is forbidden to put on tefillin on the day of burial itself, and likewise it is forbidden to put on tefillin on the day one learns of a relative's death ("close news"). But if the relative died during a festival — in which case the counting of the seven days of mourning begins only after the festival — the mourner is obligated to put on tefillin already on the first day of mourning. The custom in Jerusalem and Baghdad was that the mourner does put on the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam (contrary to the Chida's view that it is preferable not to put on tefillin at all — "sitting and not acting is preferable").
takeaways: A mourner does not put on tefillin on the first day of mourning (the day of burial, even if different from the day of death), nor on the day he learns of his relative's death ("close news"); but if the relative died during a festival, he is obligated to put on tefillin already on the first day of mourning.
The accepted custom (contrary to the Chida's view) is that the mourner does put on the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam.

paragraphs: It is forbidden to hold the tefillin suspended, whether the boxes or the straps. Even at the time of putting them on, one should be stringent not to hold only the knot while the box hangs suspended until he places it on his head; rather, he should take the knot together with the box in his hand, place the box in its place, and only afterward the knot in its place.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to hold the tefillin suspended in the air by the strap alone — neither the boxes nor the straps. Even at the time of putting them on, one should be stringent not to hold only the knot while the box hangs suspended, but rather to hold the knot together with the box in his hand, place the box in its place, and only afterward secure the knot in its place.
takeaways: One must not put on the tefillin in a manner where the box hangs suspended, supported only by the strap; one should place them together — the box first, then secure the knot.

paragraphs: When placing the tefillin into their bag, or when winding the cord at the mouth of the bag, one should not wind the bag containing the tefillin around the cord, but rather wind the cord around the bag, as noted by the later authorities. Some are also careful regarding the outer bag in which the large tallit and the tefillin bag are kept — one should be careful regarding this outer bag, in which the large tallit and the tefillin bag are placed, not to place the large tallit and the prayer book above the tefillin, but rather to place the tefillin to the side. One should also be careful, in a case where the head-tefillin and hand-tefillin are both placed in one bag, to feel them while they are still inside the bag, so as to know which is the hand-tefillin and take it out first, and not mistakenly take out the head-tefillin first. And if one wears both Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam tefillin together, in which case he must necessarily make one bag for the hand-tefillin and one bag for the head-tefillin, he should be careful to make a distinguishing mark on the bags, so that he takes out the hand-tefillin first.

clarification.explanation: When placing the tefillin into their bag and winding the cord at the bag's opening, one should wind the cord around the bag, not the bag around the cord. Some are also careful regarding the outer bag in which the large tallit and the tefillin bag are kept, not to place the tallit and the prayer book above the tefillin, but rather to place the tefillin to the side. One must also be careful, when the head-tefillin and hand-tefillin are kept together in one bag, to feel for them while still inside the bag, in order to identify the hand-tefillin (so as to take it out first, not mistakenly taking out the head-tefillin first). One who wears both Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam tefillin, and must therefore use two separate bags, should make a distinguishing mark on the bags to know to take out the hand-tefillin first.
takeaways: One should wind the cord around the bag (not the reverse), and identify the hand-tefillin by feel before removing it from the bag, so as to take it out first.

paragraphs: One whose custom is to wear both Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam tefillin together, and who winds them together to place them in the bag, must be careful not to place the box of one pair on the ma'avarta (the strap-loop passing through the box) of the other pair, but rather to place all the boxes side by side upon the straps.

clarification.explanation: One who customarily wears both Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam tefillin together, and winds them together before placing them in the bag, must be careful not to place the box of one pair on the "ma'avarta" (the strap-loop passing through the box) of the other pair, but rather to place all the boxes side by side on the straps.
takeaways: When winding two pairs of tefillin (Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam) together, the boxes should be placed side by side, not one on top of the other's ma'avarta.

paragraphs: One must be careful not to pass gas while wearing them. One who has an ailment that causes him to pass gas should wear the tefillin only during the reading of the Shema and its blessings and the Amidah prayer, and should make an effort to restrain himself during this brief time so as not to pass gas, as noted by the later authorities, of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: One must be careful not to pass gas while wearing tefillin. One who suffers from an ailment that causes a tendency to pass gas should limit himself to wearing tefillin only during the reading of the Shema and its blessings and the Amidah prayer, making an effort to restrain himself during this brief period.
takeaways: One prone to passing gas may limit himself to wearing tefillin only during the Shema and the Amidah prayer, making an effort to restrain himself during that short time.

paragraphs: One should not let his mind wander from the tefillin, except during the time of engaging in Torah study and the time of the Amidah prayer, when he is exempt from this concern. Some cleverly write the word "tefillin" in large letters at the top and side of every page of the prayer book, to help them avoid forgetting. But they need not write this within the prayer book itself; rather, they should write it on a separate sheet of paper, at the top and sides, and the size of the paper should be slightly larger than the page of the prayer book, so that when the paper is placed inside the prayer book between the pages, the letters spelling "tefillin" remain visible to his eyes and serve him as a reminder.

clarification.explanation: One should not let his mind wander from the tefillin while wearing them, except during Torah study or the Amidah prayer, when he is exempt from this concern. Some employ a device: writing the word "tefillin" in large letters at the top and side of every page of the prayer book, as a reminder not to let their mind wander. It is preferable to write this not within the prayer book itself, but on a separate sheet, slightly larger than the pages of the prayer book, so that when placed between the pages, the word "tefillin" stands out to the eye and serves as a reminder.
takeaways: One's mind should not wander from the tefillin (except during Torah study and the Amidah prayer); it is recommended to use a separate reminder sheet (not written within the prayer book itself) bearing the word "tefillin" in large letters.

paragraphs: One whose tefillin fell from his hand — it is proper for him to fast one day on that same day; and if he cannot fast, he should redeem the fast with charity. But if they fell while still inside their bag, he need not fast, and it suffices to give one perutah (small coin) to charity. And in my holy work "Rav Pe'alim" I wrote, with Heaven's help, in a responsum, that even if they fell from a height less than ten tefachim, one should still fast one day, and not as people commonly think, that a height of ten tefachim is required.

clarification.explanation: One whose tefillin fell from his hand (while exposed, not inside their bag) — it is proper for him to fast one day on that same day; and if he cannot fast, he should redeem the fast with charity. If they fell while still inside their bag, there is no need to fast, and it suffices to give one perutah to charity. Rabbi Yosef Chaim adds a novel ruling: even if they fell from a height lower than ten tefachim (contrary to the common assumption that only a fall from ten tefachim or more requires a fast), one should still fast one day.
takeaways: An exposed fall of the tefillin from the hand (even from a low height) requires a day's fast or redemption with charity; a fall while inside the bag requires only a perutah to charity.

paragraphs: When removing his tefillin, it is good for him to fold them himself and place them in the bag, out of love for the mitzvah, and not like those who hand their tefillin to their attendant to fold — and a parallel to this we find in what our sages, of blessed memory, said regarding a Torah scroll: the one who rolls it receives a reward equal to all [the others who handled it]. One should also be careful to fold them and place them in the bag immediately, right after removing them, and not like those who remove them and set them down at their side, folding them only some moments later, for it is not respectful to the tefillin to be left lying that way. At a time when one is compelled to do so — for example, when he removes them before the Musaf prayer on Rosh Chodesh, and cannot fold them right away because he wishes to pray Musaf with the congregation — he should be careful at least not to place the box upside down, meaning with the side of the ma'avarta facing up and the body of the box facing down, but rather to place it upright, and fold it immediately after the Musaf prayer.

clarification.explanation: When removing the tefillin, it is proper for the person himself to fold them and place them in the bag, out of love for the mitzvah, rather than handing them to his attendant to fold — similar to what our sages said regarding one who rolls a Torah scroll, that he receives a reward equal to all the others. One should be careful to fold and put them into the bag immediately after removal, not leaving the tefillin set aside for a while before folding, since it is not respectful to the tefillin to be left lying that way. In a case where there is a compelling need to delay (such as removing them before the Musaf prayer on Rosh Chodesh, when one wishes to pray with the congregation and cannot fold immediately), one should be careful at least not to leave the box upside down (with the ma'avarta-side facing up), but rather to place it upright, and to fold it immediately after the Musaf prayer.
takeaways: It is preferable that the person himself fold and place his tefillin in the bag immediately after removing them, rather than leaving them set aside or handing them to someone else.
